# Cinematic Scene Language

Use this reference for composition, camera, lighting, color, atmosphere, and visual hierarchy.

## Composition

Design the image in readable layers:

- Foreground: frame, obstruction, texture, threshold, figure, tool, plants, debris, window, vehicle.
- Midground: main action or hero architecture.
- Background: world scale, skyline, mountains, weather, ruins, industry, celestial body.

Use one main focal path:

- Light path: brightest value leads to the subject.
- Shape path: arches, roads, rivers, cables, smoke, stairways, trees, shadows.
- Human path: figures look, walk, work, worship, flee, wait, or point toward the focal idea.

Use negative space deliberately. Empty sky, mist, water, snow, wall, or shadow can make a scene feel expensive and controlled.

## Camera

Choose camera language based on emotional intent:

- Low angle: monumentality, intimidation, sacred scale.
- Eye level: realism, presence, documentary intimacy.
- High angle: vulnerability, tactical overview, social order, urban systems.
- Wide lens feel: spatial immersion, strong perspective, viewer inside the scene.
- Long lens feel: compressed depth, surveillance, ritual distance, painterly layering.
- Symmetrical frontal framing: ceremony, power, institutional control.
- Off-axis framing: tension, discovery, instability, realism.

Avoid overdescribing technical lens data unless the model or user benefits from it. "Wide-angle street-level view" is often better than unsupported exact millimeters.

## Lighting

Use motivated light:

- Sun, moon, fire, lantern, neon, window, temple lamp, searchlight, screen glow, welding arc, lightning, reflected water, emergency beacon.

Choose one dominant lighting strategy:

- Soft diffused overcast: realism, melancholy, quiet detail.
- Hard raking sunlight: texture, heat, severity, late-afternoon drama.
- Chiaroscuro: moral tension, sacred drama, mystery.
- Backlight and haze: silhouette, scale, mythic reveal.
- Practical pools of light: human intimacy within a large dark world.
- Color contrast: warm human space vs cool exterior, toxic green industry vs clean blue moonlight, red ceremony vs grey rain.

## Color Script

Use 3-5 color roles:

- Dominant environment hue.
- Light color.
- Shadow color.
- Accent color for the focal object.
- Skin/signage/fire/plant color if needed.

Premium color direction usually limits saturation. Let one accent carry attention instead of making every object loud.

## Atmosphere and Depth

Depth cues:

- Overlap.
- Scale falloff.
- Value separation.
- Atmospheric haze.
- Texture reduction in distance.
- Repeated forms becoming smaller.
- Warm/cool separation.
- Cast shadows that reveal terrain.

Weather should change behavior:

- Rain creates reflections, umbrellas, drainage, wet fabric, steam, darker stone.
- Snow mutes sound, hides edges, shows tracks, accumulates on windward surfaces.
- Dust reveals shafts of light, neglect, construction, deserts, archives.
- Fog simplifies silhouettes and makes lights bloom.

## Production-Design Detail

Use set dressing to tell class, labor, and history:

- Elite spaces: controlled symmetry, rare materials, hidden service routes, polished surfaces with selective wear.
- Working spaces: improvised storage, repair marks, tool logic, signage, safety systems, residue.
- Sacred spaces: thresholds, offerings, orientation, cleaning rituals, restricted zones, acoustic emptiness.
- Abandoned spaces: water damage, plant succession, stolen materials, collapsed systems, faded authority.
- Near-future spaces: old infrastructure plus selective advanced technology, not uniformly new surfaces.

## Image-Model Clarity

For generation prompts:

- Put the subject and scene type in the first sentence.
- State the camera and composition before detailed decoration.
- Group materials and lighting together.
- Avoid contradictory style commands.
- Avoid too many named references.
- Avoid requesting exact readable text unless the image model is known to handle typography.
